Merge Pending: Code Review Queues Are Engineering's Most Expensive Line Item

Editorial review against the empirical-skeptic rubric.
Post: viney.ca/review/review-queue-throughput-tax-42d2fbb4, by Ouray Viney, dated 29 Jul 2026, 6 min read.
Reviewed 29 Jul 2026. All six cited sources fetched and read; two read as raw page text after summarisation proved incomplete.

1. Verdict

BLOCK
Weighted score 51.0 / 100. Two gates fail. Even with all gates passing, 51 sits in REWORK territory (below 65).

2. Gate findings

G1: Source resolvability FAIL

G1.a  154 per cent PR size figure confidence 90%
"those same squads absorbed a 91 per cent increase in PR review time and a 154 per cent surge in average PR size"

The 91 per cent figure is on the cited Faros page. The 154 per cent figure is not. I read the full page text at faros.ai/ai-productivity-paradox and queried it specifically for any PR size statistic. The page carries 98 per cent (PRs merged), 21 per cent (tasks completed), 91 per cent (review times), and the statement that DORA metrics "remain largely unchanged." There is no PR size figure of any value.

Nor is it in the article's own chart, which plots something else entirely (see G2.g). Status: UNVERIFIED. Most likely it comes from a fuller Faros asset or a superseded version of the page, but an empirical-skeptic post cannot ship a number that a reader following the citation cannot find.

G1.b  1,055 and 201 minute pickup times confidence 85%
"Agentic AI PRs ... sit idle for 1,055 minutes before anyone opens them, against 201 minutes for unassisted work."

The cited LinearB page is a landing page gated by repeated "Download your free copy" calls to action. It publishes ratios, not absolute minutes: "AI PRs wait 4.6x longer before review" and "Agentic AI PRs have a PR Pickup Time 5.3x longer than Unassisted ones." Neither 1,055 nor 201 appears anywhere publicly reachable. Status: UNVERIFIED.

These are probably in the gated PDF, which is why my confidence is 85 rather than higher. But the citation as printed sends the reader to a page that cannot confirm the two numbers the article's only chart is built from.

G1.c  The cost of a senior engineer hour confidence 100%
"a principal or staff engineer whose hour costs an employer fifty pounds or more on any conservative reckoning"

No source, and this figure is load-bearing: it is the only monetary input in a post whose title claims to identify engineering's most expensive line item. "On any conservative reckoning" is doing the work a citation should do.

Two further problems. First, the currency is wrong for the evidence base: every dataset in the post (Graphite, LinearB, Faros, DORA) is US-centric, and the author is Canadian. Second, 50 pounds per hour is not conservative so much as simply low. A UK principal engineer on 110,000 pounds, loaded at 1.4x across roughly 1,800 productive hours, costs about 86 pounds per hour:

110,000 × 1.4 = 154,000 fully loaded
154,000 ÷ 1,800 h = 85.6 /h  (vs. 50 stated)

Understating the input weakens the author's own case, so this is not thesis-favouring. It is still an unsourced number carrying a titular claim.

G2: Citation fidelity FAIL

G2.a  The nine hour baseline is misdescribed confidence 95%
"A median pull request requiring a review takes 14 hours to merge, according to Graphite Research, against nine hours for one merged without review"

Graphite's own TL;DR, read directly from the page:

"The median active developer's PR is merged 9 hours after publishing. When excluding PRs merged without any reviews, the median developer's time to merge increases 55%, from 9 to 14 hours."

The 9 hour figure is the median across all of an active developer's PRs, reviewed and unreviewed together. It is not the median for PRs merged without review, which is what the post says it is. The true no-review median is unpublished and necessarily lower than 9 hours, since removing the unreviewed PRs from the pool pushes the median up to 14.

Note the direction: the post's error understates the gap it wants to dramatise. The 55 per cent is Graphite's own number, correctly reproduced. This is a precision failure, not a spin failure, but the denominator is wrong as printed.

G2.b  A predictor ranking the source does not make confidence 90%
"PR size, author seniority, and lines changed all trail behind review presence as predictors of cycle time."

Graphite's actual ranked list, verbatim from the page, of factors that most affect time to merge once you limit to reviewed PRs: time to first review, the number of reviews, the number of lines modified in the PR, company size.

  • "Author seniority" does not appear anywhere in the source. It is attributed to a ranking that does not contain it.
  • "PR size" and "lines changed" are the same variable, Graphite's "lines modified", listed twice as though they were two independent predictors.
  • Two factors that are in the source and rank above lines modified, time to first review and number of reviews, go unmentioned. Both would have strengthened the post's queue thesis considerably.

A rule-of-three construction has here produced an invented predictor and a duplicate. The source supports the headline claim that review presence dominates; it does not support the specific ranking asserted.

G2.c  An organisational conclusion imported into a paper that does not reach it confidence 85%
"Engineers generated substantially more code; the queue absorbed the surplus and returned nothing measurable at the organisational level."

This sits in the paragraph reporting arXiv 2607.01904 and reads as that paper's finding. It is not. The paper reports per-capita throughput (2.09x), per-reviewer load roughly doubling, automated review overtaking human review, and that "merge and revert rates held steady." It reports no organisation-level delivery outcome at all: no DORA metrics, no lead time, no delivery velocity. The "nothing measurable at the organisational level" claim belongs to Faros and DORA and has been transplanted into a citation that cannot carry it.

G2.d  A "blunt conclusion" the authors do not state confidence 70%
"The authors drew a blunt conclusion: the review pipeline, not code-writing speed, is the operative constraint on delivery."

The abstract does not state this. It describes review being restructured around automation, with per-reviewer load doubling. The paper's title, "AI Writes Faster Than Humans Can Review," clearly gestures at the claim, which is why confidence is 70 rather than higher; the full text may well argue it explicitly. But "the authors drew a blunt conclusion" is a specific attribution, and it is being hung on a title rather than on a quoted finding.

G2.e  The qualifier removed from the headline statistic confidence 95%

The post's opening statistic is LinearB's 4.6x pickup delay. LinearB states it as one sentence:

"AI PRs wait 4.6x longer before review, but are reviewed 2x faster once picked up."

The post takes the first clause and drops the second. The omitted half is directly material: it partially offsets the queue penalty that the entire article is built on, and it comes from the same sentence of the same source. This is the single most consequential fidelity defect in the piece, because the counter-evidence was not merely available, it was inside the quotation being used.

G2.f  Per cent presented as percentage points confidence 80%
"A 25-percentage-point rise in AI tool adoption correlates with an estimated 1.5 per cent decrease in software delivery throughput and a 7.2 per cent decrease in stability."

The 1.5 and 7.2 figures are correct and verified. The framing is not. RedMonk's wording is "if AI adoption increases by 25%", which is ambiguous between a relative increase and a percentage-point increase, and RedMonk does not disambiguate. The post silently resolves the ambiguity into the more precise-sounding "25-percentage-point", which the source does not license. The post's "correlates with an estimated" is otherwise a fair rendering of DORA's model-based "is expected to."

G2.g  The chart does not show what the text says it shows confidence 98%
"The chart below makes clear, however, that those same squads absorbed a 91 per cent increase in PR review time and a 154 per cent surge in average PR size"

I rendered the page and inspected the chart. It is titled "The queue, not the commit", subtitled "Median minutes a pull request waits before a reviewer opens it, by authorship type", and plots exactly two bars: Unassisted PRs at 201 minutes and Agentic AI PRs at 1,055 minutes. It contains neither the 91 per cent review-time increase nor the 154 per cent PR size surge. It is LinearB pickup data, not Faros review-time data.

It is also not "below" the sentence in any useful sense: it renders at the very bottom of the article, after the final paragraph and immediately above the References heading, roughly three sections past the reference to it. A reader who follows the pointer finds an unrelated chart. The chart additionally carries no source attribution and its accessible name is the bare string "Chart", which is an alt-text failure.

G3: Arithmetic integrity PASS

Every figure that can be recomputed reproduces. Shown rather than asserted:

Review penalty
14 h ÷ 9 h = 1.5556 → +55.6% → stated as "55 per cent"  reproduces (rounded down, against thesis)

AI PR rework share
100% − 32.7% = 67.3%; two in three = 66.67%; 67.3 > 66.67
→ "more than two in three"  reproduces

Agents below signal threshold
12 ÷ 13 = 0.92308 → 92.31%, stated as "92.3 per cent"  reproduces exactly

Code review agent study, rounding
45.20 → 45.2  |  68.37 → 68.4  |  34.88 → 34.9  |  21.60 → 21.6  all correct

Pickup multiple, internal consistency
1,055 ÷ 201 = 5.2488 → 5.25x, which rounds to 5.2x
LinearB publishes 5.3x; 201 × 5.3 = 1,065.3 ≠ 1,055; 1,055 ÷ 5.3 = 199.1 ≠ 201
→ discrepancy of about 10 minutes, consistent with rounding of the underlying values

Output multiple
2.09x stated as "twice the historical rate"  reproduces (rounded down)

Rounding direction audit. The rubric asks whether rounding consistently favours the thesis. It does not. 55.6 to 55, 5.25x to "five times", and 2.09x to "twice" all round against the argument being made. This is genuine discipline and it materially raised my confidence that the numbers were handled rather than generated.

Why this passes despite the missing cost model. G3 fails when a stated calculation does not reproduce. Here no cost calculation exists to check: the post writes "Multiply across a fifty-person organisation" and then does not multiply. That is a scope and title-fidelity failure, charged under G1.c and dimension 6, not an arithmetic error. The one real discrepancy, 5.25x against a published 5.3x, is a rounding artifact and does not rise to a gate failure.

G4: No fabrication PASS, conditional

All six sources exist and were read. Both arXiv papers are real, correctly titled, correctly attributed, and their numbers match to the decimal place:

  • arXiv 2607.01904, He, Agarwal, Denisov-Blanch, Azaletskiy, Koyejo, Vasilescu, submitted 2 Jul 2026. 802 developers, 196,212 PRs, Jan 2024 to Apr 2026, 2.09x baseline. Every parameter in the post checks out.
  • arXiv 2604.03196, Chowdhury, Banik, Ferdous, Shamim. 3,109 PRs, 19,450 comments, 45.20 vs 68.37 per cent merge, 34.88 vs 21.60 per cent abandonment, 12 of 13 agents below a 60 per cent signal ratio. Every figure checks out.

No invented quotation, person, company anecdote, or internal metric anywhere in the piece. That is a real strength and it is the main reason this post is blocked on rigour rather than on honesty.

The conditional. The 154 per cent PR size figure (G1.a) cannot at present be distinguished from invention, which is the literal G4 trigger. I am passing the gate because the leading hypothesis is provenance, not fabrication: three of the four figures attributed to that same Faros page verified exactly, which is not the pattern of a pipeline inventing statistics. If the author cannot produce a locatable source for 154 per cent, this converts to a G4 failure, which is a considerably more serious finding than the G1 failure it currently sits under.

4. The strongest objection

DORA reversed the throughput finding seven months before this post published, and the same analyst at the same publication wrote it up.

The post's causal engine is that flooding the intake without widening the review throat makes delivery slower. Its empirical anchor for the "slower" half is DORA 2024 via RedMonk: a 25 per cent rise in AI adoption associated with a 1.5 per cent throughput decrease. The post then treats this as the settled state of the evidence, twice, and rests its climax on it: "an AI productivity narrative that the DORA data refuse to validate."

DORA 2025, published 18 December 2025 and analysed by Rachel Stephens at RedMonk, the same author whose 2024 piece the post cites:

"Usage increased. Also over the year, AI's relationship with throughput shifted from negative to positive."

Nearly 5,000 respondents. AI adoption is now associated with higher delivery throughput. The single load-bearing statistic behind the post's central mechanism has been superseded by its own source lineage, and the post neither cites nor acknowledges the update. A reader who checks the citation trail one step further than the post did arrives at the opposite conclusion, which is the specific failure mode an empirical-skeptic brand cannot absorb.

What makes this objection genuinely interesting rather than merely fatal: DORA 2025 did not reverse the stability finding. Stability remains negatively associated with AI adoption, with more rework and more change failures, and DORA added a Rework Rate metric in response. So the honest 2026 version of this post is not "the queue makes delivery slower." It is closer to AI adoption now buys throughput and pays for it in stability and rework, and the review queue is where that bill arrives. That thesis survives every source in the piece, including the ones that currently contradict it, and it is a better argument than the one on the page.

Second objection: the review penalty is substantially a selection effect

The post reads Graphite's 9-versus-14 hour gap as the cost of review: "a 55 per cent penalty for the privilege of a second opinion." That treats which PRs get reviewed as random. Graphite's own companion research shows it is anything but:

  • "13% of all PRs merged by active committers since 2023 are merged without any reviews", but "the median developer merges just 0.6% of their PRs without review."
  • "15% of developers are responsible for 83% of all PRs merged without review."
  • "The median engineer at an org with 50+ committers merges <0.5% of their PRs without any review", against 5 per cent at orgs of 11 to 20 committers.
  • From the cited page itself: "Developers who merge more frequently also tend to merge faster and merge more often without waiting for reviews."

The unreviewed population is a small, highly concentrated tail of prolific committers at small organisations. The gap between it and everything else measures who skips review and on what, at least as much as it measures what review costs. The post's own primary source contains the material to complicate its headline number, and the post does not use it.

Credit where it is due. The post does anticipate and dispatch the most obvious objection, that automated reviewers can absorb the load, and it does so with the best evidence in the piece: a real study, precisely quoted, showing agent-only PRs merging at 45.2 against 68.4 per cent and 12 of 13 agents below a 60 per cent signal ratio. That section is the article working as intended.

5. Fixes, ranked

Fix 1. Address the DORA 2025 reversal. Highest impact by a wide margin.

Location: "Automation as a False Escape Route", the DORA paragraph, and the closing clause "an AI productivity narrative that the DORA data refuse to validate."

Problem: The load-bearing throughput statistic is superseded. Fixes gate G2, dimension 1 and dimension 2 at once, and strengthens rather than weakens the piece.

Replacement for the DORA passage:

Google's 2024 DORA report, analysed by RedMonk's Rachel Stephens, found that a 25 per cent rise in AI adoption was associated with an estimated 1.5 per cent decrease in delivery throughput and a 7.2 per cent decrease in stability. That finding has since been half-retracted by its own authors, and the half that survived is the more damaging one. DORA 2025, drawing on nearly 5,000 respondents, reports that AI's relationship with throughput "shifted from negative to positive" over the year. Adoption now moves work through the system faster. What did not shift is stability: AI adoption remains associated with rising instability, more change failures and more rework, to the point that DORA added a Rework Rate metric to track it.

That revision does not rescue the queue. It relocates the bill. Throughput gains are real and now measurable; they are being financed by rework and instability, and rework is precisely what returns to the review queue for a second pass. The 2024 reading was that AI adoption made delivery slower. The 2026 reading is narrower and harder to dismiss: AI adoption buys throughput on credit, and the review queue is where the interest is charged.

Requires retitling the section, since automation is no longer purely a false escape route, and adjusting the closing clause: "an AI productivity narrative that the DORA data validate only on throughput, and refuse to validate on anything that happens after the merge."

Fix 2. Build the ledger the title promises, or change the title.

Location: "Reviewing the Reviewer Problem", the "fifty pounds" passage.

Problem: G1.c plus the dimension 6 title failure. The post claims stark unit economics and unforgiving arithmetic, then performs none. Fixing this also lifts dimension 4, since a costed model is itself decision-relevant.

Replacement:

Put a number on it. Take a fifty-engineer organisation with ten senior reviewers, and assume each spends five hours a week in review, which is conservative against Faros's reported 91 per cent increase in review time. At LinearB's 32.7 per cent acceptance rate for AI-generated PRs, roughly two thirds of the time spent on that cohort buys nothing that ships.

Ten reviewers × 5 h/week × 67.3 per cent wasted = 33.7 reviewer-hours a week.
Across 46 working weeks: 1,550 hours.
At a fully loaded principal-engineer cost of 85 dollars an hour: 132,000 dollars a year, or about 0.8 full-time senior engineers.

Every input there is an assumption and the output should be read as an order of magnitude, not an invoice. Note what it shows: against a fifty-person payroll, this is under one per cent of engineering cost. The review queue is not the most expensive line item on the ledger. It is something more awkward: an unbudgeted charge levied specifically against the people whose attention is hardest to replace, and it appears on no dashboard at all.

This kills the current title. It should. "Most Expensive Line Item" is not defensible at any plausible set of inputs and it is the kind of claim this audience will run the numbers on. Suggested replacement, which the body actually delivers: "Merge Pending: The Review Queue Is Where AI's Productivity Gains Go To Die", or, closer to the revised thesis, "Merge Pending: AI Buys Throughput On Credit, And Review Is Where The Bill Lands".

Fix 3. Restore LinearB's second clause.

Location: Opening paragraph, the 4.6x statistic.

Problem: G2.e. Deleting the offsetting half of a quoted sentence is the defect most corrosive to an empirical-skeptic brand, and it is trivially fixable.

According to LinearB's 2026 Software Engineering Benchmarks Report, which analysed 8.1 million pull requests across more than 4,800 organisations, AI-assisted PRs wait 4.6 times longer for a reviewer to pick them up than manually written code. They are then reviewed about twice as fast once someone opens them, which tells you the delay is not comprehension difficulty. It is queueing. The wait is not in the reading; it is in the waiting to be read.

The omitted clause, restored, is better evidence for the thesis than its absence was. Fast review of long-queued PRs is exactly what a capacity constraint looks like rather than a complexity one.

Fix 4. Correct the Graphite denominator and the predictor list.

Location: Opening paragraph.

Problem: G2.a and G2.b. Two defects, one of which asserts a predictor ("author seniority") absent from the source.

Graphite Research puts the median active developer's pull request at 9 hours from publish to merge. Strip out the PRs merged with no review at all and that median rises 55 per cent, to 14 hours. Reviews, in Graphite's own ranking, are the single largest determinant of time to merge, ahead of the number of reviews, the lines modified, and company size. Keyboards are not the constraint. Queues are.

One caveat the data demand: PRs that skip review are not a random sample. Graphite finds that 13 per cent of merged PRs go unreviewed, but the median developer accounts for 0.6 per cent of them, and 15 per cent of developers account for 83 per cent. The unreviewed pool is a narrow tail of prolific committers at smaller organisations. Some of that 55 per cent is what review costs; some is who skips it. Treat it as an upper bound on the review penalty, not a measurement of it.

The caveat costs the post nothing rhetorically and buys most of the dimension 2 deficit back, because it demonstrates knowing which way the citation is wrong. That is the exact move the evidence anchor rewards at 4.

Fix 5. Fix the chart, or delete the sentence pointing at it.

Location: Faros paragraph, and the chart at the foot of the article.

Problem: G2.g. The text sends the reader to a chart showing different data, three sections away.

Three things to do:

  • Move the chart up to the Faros paragraph, or point to it accurately. Since it plots LinearB pickup minutes, it belongs beside the 4.6x discussion in the opening, not beside the Faros percentages.
  • Rewrite the referring sentence so it describes the chart it actually has: "Those same squads absorbed a 91 per cent increase in PR review time with no measurable improvement in deployment frequency, lead time, or change failure rate." No chart reference, and no 154 per cent (see Fix 6).
  • Add a source line to the chart ("Source: LinearB, 2026 Software Engineering Benchmarks Report") and real alt text, currently the bare string "Chart". Suggested: "Bar chart: median minutes before a reviewer opens a PR. Unassisted 201 minutes; agentic AI 1,055 minutes."

Fix 6. Source or cut the 154 per cent, and source the pickup minutes.

Location: Faros paragraph; the chart.

Problem: G1.a and G1.b, and the conditional on G4.

  • 154 per cent: not on the cited page. Either cite the specific Faros asset and page it appears on, or cut it. Do not leave it standing on a URL that does not contain it. If no source can be produced, this becomes a fabrication finding, so resolve it explicitly rather than quietly deleting it.
  • 1,055 and 201 minutes: cite the gated report properly, with the report page or figure number, so a reader knows the numbers live behind a download rather than on the landing page. Also reconcile the rounding: as printed they yield 5.25x against LinearB's published 5.3x.

Fix 7. Add an action and a falsification condition.

Location: New closing section, before the final paragraph.

Problem: Dimension 4 at 1 out of 5, and the absence of any falsification condition under dimension 2. Worth 5 to 6 points on its own.

If the queue is the constraint, three things follow, and all three are measurable by the end of a quarter.

Instrument pickup time, not cycle time. Most engineering dashboards report time to merge, which blends queueing with review effort and hides the former inside the latter. Split them. The number that matters is median minutes from PR published to first reviewer comment, cut by authorship type. If AI-authored PRs show a materially worse pickup time than human-authored ones, you have the constraint on a chart.

Budget review capacity explicitly when you buy generation capacity. A tool rollout that raises output per engineer needs a named reviewer allocation attached to the same business case, in hours per week, owned by the engineering manager who approved the rollout. Review capacity treated as residual will be consumed as residual.

Gate on acceptance rate, not volume. At a 32.7 per cent acceptance rate for AI-generated PRs, volume of PRs opened is an actively misleading metric. Track the merge rate of AI-authored PRs per team, and treat a falling rate as a signal to slow generation rather than to add reviewers.

I would abandon this position on one piece of evidence: an organisation that materially raises per-engineer output, holds reviewer headcount flat, and still improves deployment frequency and change failure rate over two consecutive quarters. That would mean review capacity was elastic and the queue was never the binding constraint. I have not seen it published. DORA 2025's throughput reversal is the closest anyone has come, and it bought that throughput with rework, which is the queue collecting anyway.

6. What is working

Brief, as specified, and limited to what is genuinely above pipeline baseline.

  • The two arXiv citations are exemplary. Real papers, correct titles, correct author lists, and every figure accurate to the decimal place: 802 developers, 196,212 PRs, 45.20 against 68.37 per cent, 12 of 13 agents. Sourcing at this precision is rare in generated editorial and it is the reason this review reads as a rigour problem rather than an integrity problem. Keep doing exactly this.
  • Rounding discipline runs against the thesis. 55.6 to "55 per cent", 5.25x to "five times", 2.09x to "twice". A pipeline optimising for impact rounds the other way. This is the single most trust-earning property of the draft.
  • The automation counter-argument is pre-empted with the best evidence in the piece. Reaching for the code-review-agent study to close off "just use bots" is the structural move that separates an argument from an assertion, and that section is load-bearing under the delete-it test.
  • Vendor neutrality holds under pressure. Three of the four data sources sell tooling into this exact problem, and none is endorsed or even implicitly recommended. That is harder than it looks and it was done cleanly.
  • The voice is close to house best. Numbers before adjectives, short sentences carrying the claims, and a standfirst that earns its place. Dimension 5 at 4 out of 5 is the highest score here and it is not a consolation prize.
